translation:
…which discusses those who emerged [at that time]. During this period the influence of ritual actions such as yajnas and sacrifices grew. An age of various vows, fasts, and mantra-tantra practices arrived, but even so, no one could recognize Parbrahm (the Supreme Being) through them. Regarding this, Jivanji Maharaj states:

_vedaih puranair vividhaih kechid vibhranta-chetasah_
_nishchayam nadhigacchanti kim etat paramam padam_ ||41||
_kim etad vaishnavam padam_ ||
(Some people, their minds bewildered by the various Vedas and Puranas, cannot ascertain with certainty what this supreme state — this Vaishnav state — truly is.)

Some people, though their minds are fixed on Brahman, still cannot determine through the Vedas and the various Puranas what this Vaishnav state (the supreme state) actually is.

That is to say, those who try to determine the nature of Parbrahm on the basis of philosophical treatises, the Vedas, or the Puranas cannot attain Parbrahm through such knowledge or ritual action. God is not a subject of knowledge or of ritual action; God is, by nature, devotion (bhakti) itself, and can be attained only through that devotion. As for the various Puranas and philosophical schools, which themselves contradict one another — how could Parbrahm be recognized through them?

_shrutir vibhinna smritayash cha bhinna naiko munir yasya vachah pramanam_
_dharmasya tattvam nihitam guhayam mahajano yena gatah sa panthah_
(The words of scripture differ from one another, and the smritis differ too; there is not even a single sage whose word alone can be taken as authoritative. The secret of dharma lies hidden deep within a cave; therefore the path that the great ones — the saints — have walked is the path one should follow.)

The words of the shrutis are different from each other, and the smritis are different too. There is not a single sage whose word can be regarded as authoritative. The secrets of dharma lie hidden deep within a cave; therefore one should follow the path on which great saints (mahajans) have walked.

_rishirbhir bahavo loke panthanah prakatikritah_
_shrama-sadhyash cha te sarve prayah svarga-phala-pradah_ ||56||
(Bhagavat Mahatmya, chapter 2)
(The sages have made known many paths in this world, but all of them require great effort, and for the most part yield only the fruit of heaven.)

The sages have made known many paths in the world, but all of them are attained only with great hardship, and in the end they mostly grant only the attainment of heaven.

_nanudhyayed bahun shabdan tyajed granthamasheshatah_
(One should not dwell too much on many words; one should abandon scriptural texts altogether.)

The shruti says that one should not pay too much heed to many words, and should give up scriptures root and branch.

_ananta shastram bahu veditavyam alpash cha kalo bahavash cha vighnah_
_yat sarabhutam tad upasitavyam hamso yatha kshiram ivambu-mishram_
(The scriptures are endless, and much remains to be learned; but time is short and obstacles are countless. Therefore one should hold fast only to the essence — as a swan draws out only the milk from water mixed with milk.)

There is no end to the scriptures, and there is much to know, but time is very short and obstacles are without limit. Therefore, just as a swan draws only the milk out of a mixture of water and milk, wise men and women should grasp the very essence of the true religious principle and come to know it.

_na shishyan anubadhniyat granthan naivabhyased bahun_
_na vyakhyam upayunjita narambhan arabhet kvachit_
(One should not strive to gather many disciples, nor study numerous texts; one should not undertake the work of giving public discourses, nor engage in [worldly] undertakings such as founding monasteries.)

One should not make efforts to gather many disciples, nor study a great many scriptures. One should not take up the work of public discourse before assemblies, nor engage in schemes such as building monasteries. Narsinh Mehta says:

_Akhil brahmand ma ek tu Shri Hari, juj've rupe anant bhase_
_Granth garbad kari, vaat na kari kharee, jehne je game tene puje_
(In the whole universe You alone are Shri Hari, appearing endlessly in countless forms; people have muddled the scriptures and no one has spoken the real truth — everyone worships whatever pleases them.)

_santyajya sarva-shastrani santyajyamum cha sangraham_
_rita-putam manah-putah satya-putam samacharet_
(Having abandoned all scriptures, and having abandoned also whatever one has accumulated, one should act only after purifying it through good conduct, purifying it with the mind, and purifying it with truth.)

The excellent ones should abandon all scriptures, and should also give up whatever [learning] they themselves have gathered; testing it by right conduct, by the mind, and by truth — filtering it through all three — they should act accordingly.

_vag-vaishvari shabda-jhari shastra-vyakhyana-kaushalam_
_vidusham iha vaidushyam bhuktaye na muktaye_
(A flowing stream of eloquent words and skill in expounding the scriptures — such is the learning of the learned in this world; it leads only to worldly enjoyment, not to liberation.)

Adi Shankaracharya says in the Vivek Chudamani that a beautiful, graceful, continuous flow of speech and the skill of giving excellent discourses — all of this can obtain only worldly enjoyments. Through it one cannot attain liberation, that is, the lotus feet of the Lord.

_pathanti veda shastrani bodhayanti parasparam_
_na jananti param tattvam darvi paka-rasam yatha_ ||38||
(Garuda Purana, chapter 16)
(They recite the Vedas and scriptures, and instruct one another, but they do not know the supreme truth — just as a ladle does not know the taste of the dish it stirs.)

The learning of pandits is for earning a livelihood, not for liberation. Thus pandits recite the Vedas and other scriptures and instruct one another about them, but if they themselves do not understand the inner secret, they are like the ladle that keeps turning in the pot of vegetable curry — it stirs the curry this way and that, but never knows its taste. Such pandits are like that ladle.

Sawaiya:
_Aadi alif taame chit soch poch chaho nit karni kaha kaha kijiye_
_Vedanko paar nahi puranko ant nahi baani bahoteri chit kaha kaha dijiye_
_Natki kala badi chhandko prabandh bado, rangke rasile ras kaun kaun pijiye_
_Lakh baatanki ek baat Tulsi bataye det, janam sudharo to Ramnaam lijiye_
(If from the very outset we keep weighing in the mind what is good and what is bad, we will never grasp what to do at every moment, for the Vedas have no end and the Puranas have no limit, and countless other scriptures exist besides — where should the mind dwell? The skill of drama is great, the composition of poetic metres is vast, and the flavors are many — which flavor should the lovers of loving devotion drink? So out of millions of matters, Tulsidas points to just one: if you wish to make good use of this human birth, take only the name of Ram.)

If, right from the start, we keep weighing in our mind what is good and what is bad, we will never be able to grasp what to do at each moment — because there is no reaching the far end of the Vedas, no reaching the end of the Puranas, and besides these there are many more scriptures too. So where all should we keep our mind fixed? The skill of this player (Maya) who runs this world is very great indeed, and the poetic compositions are also very many; so which flavor should the connoisseurs of loving devotion drink? Therefore, out of millions of statements and facts, Tulsidas points out just the one essential matter: if you wish to make good use of your human birth, then take only the name of Ram.

_Kya kariye kya jodiye, thode jeevan kaj_
_Chhod chhod sab jaat hai, deh-geh dhan-raj_
(What should one do, what should one accumulate, for this brief span of life? Leaving it all behind, everyone departs — body, home, wealth, and kingdom.)

It is not understood what one should do and what one should gather for this short life, because everyone eventually departs, leaving behind body, home, wealth, and kingdom.

_balastavat kridasaktas tarunastavat tarunirakah_
_vriddhastavad chintamagnah pare brahmani ko'pi na lagnah_
(Charpat Manjari Stotra)
(In childhood one is absorbed in play, in youth one is enamored of a woman, and in old age one is sunk in worries — no one, at any stage, becomes attached to the supreme Brahman.)

Childhood passed away in playing with those of similar age; youth was spent lost in the enchantment of wife, children, and worldly wealth; and old age was besieged by worries — but at no stage could one manage to worship Brahman.

_Tulsi Sitaramkun, reejh bhajo ke kheej_
_Ulta sulta boiye, jyun khet mein beej_
(Tulsidas says: worship Sita-Ram whether with joy or with irritation — for just as a seed sown in a field, whether right side up or upside down, still sprouts.)

Tulsidas says, do the bhajan of Sitaram with love or even in anger — for just as a seed sown in a field, whether sown the right way up or upside down, still sprouts, in the same way the bhajan of Ram never goes to waste.

_Uthat bethat jeevna, samro Sitaram_
_Sant samagam jheelvo, nahi sovanko kaam_
(Whether rising or sitting, O soul, remember Sita-Ram; immerse yourself in the company of saints — this is no time for negligence.)

Jivanji Maharaj says: whether rising or sitting, keep remembering Sitaram at every moment, and keep good company with the saints; carelessness now will not bring deliverance.

Therefore Jivanji Maharaj says: life is short, but the ocean to be churned is vast — meaning, during such a brief lifespan, if one first has to study all these scriptures, Puranas, Upanishads, tantra texts and so on, and only then search for the truth, then when could it ever be found? For if one wishes to churn the whole ocean, how enormous would the churning-rod need to be, and how long the rope? Thus, by groping about here and there in this way, one's life comes to an end, yet Parbrahm still cannot be attained, and one has to keep circling again and again in this same cycle of birth and death. That is why it is said:

_tula-purusha-danadyaih ashvamedhadikair makhaih_
_Varanasi-Prayagadi-tirthair bhakteh na samam Ramanamnah syat_ ||42||
(Not by gifts such as tula-purush-dan, nor by sacrifices such as the ashvamedha, nor by pilgrimages to Varanasi, Prayag and the like, is there anything equal to devotion to the Name of Ram.)

Give the tula-purush gift and other gifts, perform sacrifices such as the ashvamedha, and go on pilgrimage to Varanasi, Prayag, and other holy places — still, there is nothing equal to devotion.

That is to say, whether one performs various kinds of gifts such as tula-dan (going to a pilgrimage site or temple and donating an item whose weight equals one's own body weight), or other gifts, or performs the various sacrifices prescribed in the Purva Mimamsa, or bathes in rivers considered sacred such as the Ganga, or goes to Gaya and performs the shraddha rites and so on, or visits various holy pilgrimage places, or keeps vows and fasts — without devotion, liberation, that is, Parbrahm, cannot be attained.

Among the sixteen kinds of great gifts (mahadan), the very first is tula-dan. The Parashar Smriti describes the procedure for it thus:

_pilyakaksham tatha chamam takram chodaka-saktavah_
_tri-ratram upavasash cha tulapurusha uchyate_ ||79||
(Parashar Smriti, 12.)
(Eating oil-cake residue for one day, sour rice-water the next, buttermilk the next, water the next, roasted-grain flour the next, and fasting for three nights — this eight-day observance is called Tulapurush.)

For one day eat oil-cake residue, for one day drink the water in which rice has been washed, for one day drink buttermilk, for one day drink only water, for one day eat roasted-grain flour, and for three nights observe a fast — this eight-day vow is called Tulapurush. It is said regarding the receiver of the gift that by accepting gifts and the like (pratigraha), the hands become scorched, and by speaking falsehood or improper words, the speech becomes scorched, that is, corrupted. In such a person, no valor or inner strength remains. If there is no valor or strength in the receiver of the gift, what benefit is there in giving the gift? Adhyaruji has said much about giving.

_Yaag daan ne vrat tape, mujh talta naahi avtaar_
(By sacrifice, gift-giving, vows and austerities, my cycle of birth and death does not end.)

By sacrifice, gift-giving, vows and austerities, my cycle of birth and death does not end — because:

_Yaag daanadike raaj prapt hoye, dharm khoote ne adhomukh pade_
(Through sacrifice, gift-giving and the like one may obtain a kingdom such as heaven, but once the merit is exhausted, one falls headlong back into birth and death.)

Through such sacrifice, gift-giving and the like, a heavenly kingdom may be obtained, but once the merit runs out, one has to fall headlong back into birth and death — because:

_Yaag daan adhyatm nathi garbhno paar-paaye_
(Sacrifice, gift-giving, and spiritual knowledge do not, [by themselves], put an end to dwelling in the womb, i.e., to rebirth.)

Even performing sacrifice, gift-giving, or spiritual and Brahma-knowledge, one does not come to the end of dwelling in the womb [i.e., of being born again].

Here again the question arises: why devotion alone? Can Parbrahm not be attained without devotion, through the paths described above?

As we have already seen earlier, devotion is a more direct and simple path than the various other paths. Moreover, there is no pretense or ostentation in devotion, nor does the practice of devotion require knowledge or scholarship. On this path there is no possibility of going astray.

_Gaaine vaaine kai nav jaanu, Hari Hari Ramji vakhaanu re ruda ek chante e_ ||1||
_Govind gaata laagi re khaant, Hari Hari bhraant bhaagi bhav kodtani_ ||2||
_Vishnu bhakti vina je kashun jeeve, Hari Hari haath divdo ne andh kuve pade e_ ||42||
(I know nothing at all of singing hymns and playing music; I only praise Hari, Hari, the good Lord Ram, with a single-pointed mind. ||1|| By singing of Govind a longing was kindled in me; the illusion of crores of worldly births was destroyed, O Hari, Hari. ||2|| Whoever lives without devotion to Vishnu is like a blind man who, even with a lamp in hand, still falls into a well, O Hari, Hari. ||42||)

(From Adhyaruji's kirtan, 27-1-11)
That is, Adhyaruji Maharaj says: I know nothing of the verses of the Vedas or hymns and the like, nor of rosaries and such observances; I only praise the practice of devotion to the excellent Ram with single-pointed faith. Practicing devotion to God filled me with zeal, and the fear of wandering through the ocean of worldly existence for millions of lifetimes has left me. Therefore, whoever lives their life without devotion to God (Vishnu) is like a blind man who, even carrying a lamp in his hand, still falls into a well — in the same way, without devotion to God, we too will fall into the ocean of worldly existence.

_Gaya shraddhadibhir api veda-pathadibhir japaih_
_tapobhir ugrair niyamaih na samam Ramanamnah syat_ ||43||
(Not even by performing shraddha rites at Gaya, by recitation of the Vedas, by japa, by fierce austerities, or by [ascetic] observances, is there anything equal to the Name of Ram.)

Perform shraddha and the like at Gaya and elsewhere, recite the Vedas, do japa, undertake severe austerities, or observe [ascetic] disciplines — still there is nothing like the Name of Ram.

Jivanji Maharaj says: study the Vedas and the many scriptures and Puranas, observe celibacy (brahmacharya) — even so, liberation is not attained without the substance of devotion. Moreover, following the conventional [ritual] path, wearing tilak and tulsi [beads], chanting the hymns of the Vedas and the like, [performing] pilgrimages, vows, sacrifices, japa, charitable and meritorious deeds, water-offerings, and teaching — all of these are [merely] ritual action (karma). Therefore, even while practicing devotion to Vishnu in this ritual-bound way, liberation is not attained. Only devotion free of [attachment to] ritual action — a true Vaishnav state — is genuine devotion. What, then, is such devotion? The Bhagavat Mahatmya, chapter 2, verse 21, gives the essence of it:

_alam vratair alam tirthair alam yogair alam makhaih_
_alam jnana-katha-lapair bhaktir ekaiva mukti-da_ ||21||
(Enough of vows, enough of pilgrimages, enough of yoga, enough of sacrifices, enough of discourses on [theoretical] knowledge — devotion alone is what grants liberation.)

Enough, enough — there is no need for so many means such as vows, pilgrimage, yoga, sacrifice, and discussions of [theoretical] knowledge. Devotion alone is what grants liberation.
